en.title: A read-only prompt that makes every bot prove its work before you trust it
en.summary: The author shares a read-only setup prompt for applying a reliability and trust standard across a Grok Bot team: each bot should leave independently checkable evidence that a job is complete, rather than just saying it is done. That evidence standard is the author's stated design, not a product behavior tested in this review.
en.whyItWorks: The author argues that trust comes from making a bot's work checkable, so you trust the evidence rather than the bot. The prompt itself starts as a read-only review and waits for approval before changing instructions, permissions, routines, memories or workflows. Whether a given setup can actually require that evidence was not independently tested here.
workflowSteps: As described by the author, start with a read-only review. The prompt tells the bot not to change instructions, permissions, routines, memories or workflows without your approval.

As described by the author, define independently checkable evidence for each recurring job (examples in the prompt include a Notion record, a sent email ID, a screenshot, a verified result, or a count of processed items). A bot saying “Done” is not treated as proof. Map facts that can change to an authoritative source, and document three boundaries for each bot: what it may do alone, what needs your approval, and what it must never do.

As described by the author, failures should be visible (what went wrong, what was tried, what actually finished, and what needs you), with one safe retry then a stop rather than an unapproved workaround; repeated corrections become proposed instruction changes for you to approve.

As described by the author, pilot one bot on one real, low-risk workflow, or propose a test for your approval if live testing is not authorised. Review the report and the first proposed changes, and approve them before anything is applied or extended to the rest of the team.
en.promptTemplate:
Help me introduce a reliability and trust standard across my entire Grok Bot team.

Start with a read-only review. Do not change any instructions, permissions, routines, memories or workflows without my approval.

1 - Make every Bot prove its work.

For each recurring job, define what evidence must be provided before the job can be considered complete.

Examples include a Notion record, a sent email ID, a screenshot, a verified result or a count of processed items.

A Bot saying 'Done' is not proof. The evidence must be independently checkable.

2 - Stop trusting memory for changing information.

Identify which Bots rely on information that can change, including dates, prices, balances, deadlines and task statuses.

Map each fact to its authoritative source.

Require a fresh source check when the information needs to be current. Reuse checks when appropriate to avoid unnecessary usage.

If a source is unavailable, report that rather than guessing.

3 - Define exactly what each Bot is allowed to do.

For every Bot, document three categories:

What it can do independently.
What requires my approval.
What it must never do.

Flag unclear boundaries and ask me to resolve them. 

Preserve existing permissions.

4 - Make failures visible.

Create a clear failure-handling rule for each Bot.

When something fails, it should explain what went wrong, what it attempted, what was actually completed and what needs my attention.

Allow one safe retry where appropriate, then stop rather than improvising an unapproved workaround.

5 - Turn corrections into permanent improvements.

Review repeated mistakes and corrections across the team.

Identify which problems could be prevented with clearer instructions, improved procedures or repeatable skills and scripts.

Propose the exact changes for my approval.

Track whether the same mistakes become less frequent over time.

6 - Make Bots earn greater independence.

For new or unreliable workflows, start with a draft-and-approve process.

Test the output against clear quality standards and require evidence of successful completion.

Only recommend greater autonomy after the Bot has demonstrated consistent performance.

Never expand permissions without my approval.

7 - Test the trust standard.

Select one Bot and one real, low-risk workflow for a pilot.

Check whether it provides completion evidence, verifies changing information, respects approval boundaries and reports failures correctly.

Where live testing isn't authorised, propose a test for my approval instead.

Return a report showing:

- Each Bot's responsibilities and trust gaps.
- Evidence required for completion.
- Source-checking and approval rules.
- Recommended instruction changes.
- Test results and outstanding risks.

Show me the proposed changes for the first Bot and wait for my approval before applying anything or extending the process to the rest of the team.

If you can't inspect a Bot's setup, tell me what you need and provide the instructions I can add manually.
en.connectorsAndRoutines: None required to start. The prompt reviews bots you already have. A Notion record or a sent email ID appear only as examples of completion evidence, not as required connectors. This review did not create a bot, routine, or connector, and did not run the prompt.

zh.title: 一条只读 Prompt：让每个 Bot 用可核对的证据证明工作，而不是口头说做完了
zh.summary: 作者分享了一条只读设置 Prompt，用于在整个 Grok Bot 团队中推行可靠性与信任标准：每个 Bot 应用可独立核对的证据证明工作已完成，而不是口头说做完了。这一证据标准是作者自述的设计，不是本轮独立测试过的产品行为。
zh.whyItWorks: 作者的主张是：信任来自让 Bot 的工作可被核对，从而信任证据而不是 Bot 本身。这条 Prompt 以只读检查开始，在改动指令、权限、例行任务、记忆或工作流之前必须等你批准。具体配置能否真正要求这些证据，本轮未独立测试。
workflowSteps: 按作者的设计，先做只读检查。这条 Prompt 要求 Bot 在未经你批准前，不改任何指令、权限、例行任务、记忆或工作流。
按作者的设计，为每项经常性工作规定可独立核对的证据（Prompt 中的例子包括 Notion 记录、已发送邮件 ID、截图、已核实的结果，或已处理条目的数量）。Bot 说 “Done” 本身不算证明。把会变化的事实对应到权威来源，并为每个 Bot 写清三类边界：可独立做的、需要你批准的、以及绝不允许做的。
按作者的设计，失败应当可见（出了什么问题、尝试了什么、实际完成了什么、需要你处理什么），必要时安全重试一次后停止，而不是未经批准自行变通；反复出现的纠正会整理成待你批准的指令修改建议。
按作者的设计，先选一个 Bot 和一项真实、低风险的工作做试点；若现场测试未获授权，则先提出测试方案等你批准。先看报告和针对第一个 Bot 的修改建议，你批准后再应用，并再推广到其余团队。

source.excerpt:
I asked my Grok Bot Chief of Staff how I could make my entire Bot team more reliable and trustworthy.

Its answer was surprisingly simple:

"You won't get trust by hoping the Bot gets smarter. You get it by making its work checkable, so you trust the evidence instead of the Bot."
